newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan finance minister expects IMF loan deal.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan finance minister expects IMF loan deal.

text.p: Pakistan's Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Tuesday he was confident that talks this week with the International Monetary Fund would result in a new medium-term loan to support his country's structural reforms.
"The structural agenda in my view is fairly well advanced, in many ways ahead of IMF initial expectations," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"On that basis I do not see any major difficulty, but we have to marry this reform agenda with a macro-economic frame which will not allow macro instability to interfere with our reform programme.
"That is going to be the main focus of this mission," he said of talks with an IMF team due in Islamabad on Wednesday.
IMF resident representative Shamsuddin Tareq said on Monday the mission would start talks on a new enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) for Pakistan.

The IMF halted a standby loan of to Pakistan in March after it became clear that agreed targets for 1996/7 could not be met. Aziz said the government's reforms in the past four months included drastic tax and tariff cuts, and reforms in the banking sector and tax collecting administration.
"We are also reviewing governmental machinery and downsizing the (public) corporations and governmental structure and we are trying to promote exports and increase agricultural production."
Aziz said the revenue and spending targets laid out in his budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) were generally consistent with the reform programme, but some fine-tuning might be needed.
The talks with the IMF mission should result in the signing of a policy framework paper at the end of July, he added.

Aziz said it was for the IMF board to determine the size of any new loan, saying it was expected to be around $1.2 billion, but argued that its symbolic importance for investors and other lenders overshadowed the actual amount of money.
"Somehow the fact that we have an arrangement with the IMF facilitates many other flows from the World Bank, the Asian (Development) Bank and many other structural facilities.

"So the package as a whole is very important in the short run while our own production and exports pick up. This will give the necessary boost in the next year or two to...build up our reserves and try to create confidence in the market," he said.
Aziz said enough medium-term financing had been arranged to ensure that Pakistan could meet its debt servicing payments of about $2.4 billion a year. "We have a breathing space," he said.

He said a combination of higher exports and the use of privatisation proceeds to retire debt should see Pakistan through the next two or three years, after which foreign investment inflows would boost the industrial growth rate.
"If our industrial exports, which were not very well in the last three years, do pick up, then we are safe as far as our debt servicing is concerned," the minister declared.
Aziz said liquid foreign reserves had risen to about $1.2 billion from about $550 million when the new government took over in February.
"There is enough cushion in our reserves to meet our obligations and with the IMF and (World) Bank and all other packages, we are all right till June next year."
